blindSummary:
This state/province adopted a state/province-level "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution in 2020, repealed on 20 September 2021 under supranational funding pressure, placing it in the same five-region configuration as the country's contiguous belt of conservative regional authorities. The declaration carried the same intent as its siblings: to exclude a visible public LGBTQ presence from the region's civic space.

Within the same unit, however, the regional capital - the country's second city - has moved decisively the other way. In May 2024 a newly elected mayor announced he would become the first holder of that office to attend the city's LGBT equality march and would fly a rainbow flag at city hall; his predecessor (2002-2024) had only become an honorary march patron in 2021 and never attended. For a visitor in the capital's old town, the operative institutional signal is the mayor's public presence, not the repealed regional document.

Legal-overview article on the rise and fall of the country's LGBT-free zones: between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 local governments adopted 'LGBT ideology'-free resolutions or family-rights charters drafted by a conservative legal institute, covering about a third of the country at the movement's peak; the documents created no criminal penalties but symbolically sidelined LGBT residents from civic life; litigation by the national human-rights commissioner led courts to strike them down as unconstitutional, a supranational funding body threatened to freeze billions in regional funds, and the last remaining zone was abolished in spring 2025.
blindTangential: Both poles - the repealed regional resolution and the capital mayor's march attendance - concern LGBT public presence broadly rather than trans status specifically; they set the general institutional climate a trans visitor reads locally, without trans-specific enforcement either way.
